newsitem.title: USA: Steve Jobs' new mission is Pixar studios.
newsitem.headline: Steve Jobs' new mission is Pixar studios.

text.p: Step into Steve Jobs' latest technology revolutionising company, Pixar Animation Studios, and you'll be struck by how untechy it seems.
Pixar produced the world's first fully computer-animated Hollywood film, the hit "Toy Story," and is said to be breaking new ground in applying computer graphics to movie making.

But inside Pixar's headquarters in this industrial city northeast of San Francisco it seems more like a preschool. Charcoal drawings of cartoon characters and photographs of bugs and plants adorn the walls. Life-size cardboard action figures stand in the hallways. Staff members arrive on bikes and work in cubicles brimming with Slinkeys, Gumby figures and Buzz Lightyear dolls.
Jobs revolutionised personal computing with his first company, Apple Computer Inc., and arguably did the same for programming with software company NeXT Computer.
Now, Jobs said, his "heart, mind and body," are at Pixar, where he spends "98 percent" of his working time.

But Pixar is very different from Apple or NeXT. Its chief operation is storytelling. And its widely acknowledged success with "Toy Story" -- the highest-grossing U.S. film released in 1995 and the third highest-grossing animated feature film ever -- will repeat itself only if the company continues to produce great theatre.
"Pixar is an entertainment company. Our product is content," Jobs said.

Thus the marriage with high technology. Mixed with the staff of artsy animators and actors is an equally large and talented staff of computer engineers. But the tech stuff is, quite literally, behind the scenes.

"Not much is known about animation and how an animated film is made because for a long time there was only Disney and Disney didn't talk about it very much," Jobs said. "In 60 years, only two studios have made blockbuster animation feature films: Walt Disney, and in December 1995 Pixar became the second."

Like at Disney, which was Pixar's distribution and marketing partner for "Toy Story" and will be in five more films over the next 10 years, the work at Pixar begins with hand drawings -- lots of them. The first two years of the four it takes to make a feature-length animated film like "Toy Story" consist of acting, story development, sketching, and studying how ordinary things move or reflect light, Jobs said.

Only after the screenplay is written, each scene drawn in long storyboards of charcoal sketches, all the settings created in pastel drawings and the characters sculpted into 3-D clay moulds do computers come into action.

Then, for sure, some pretty high-tech stuff happens. The character sculptures are digitally scanned into computers, so the animators can manipulate them to look three-dimensional. Textures, such as 15,000 hairs on a head, and colours and shades are "drawn" or rendered. Sound is added and mixed.

Pixar's technology edge for this rendering work comes from three software programmes it developed and patented. "Marionette" is its animation software for modelling, animating and lighting. "RenderMan" is a rendering system used to make photo-realistic images and image synthesis. "Ringmaster" is production management software for scheduling, coordinating and tracking a computer animated project.
The software "frees our animators from having to be great drawers, but they are brilliant actors," Jobs said. The software also frees them from having to know computers.

"I definitely am not a computer jock. I didn't really know much about computers before coming here," said Pete Doctor, Pixar's lead animator on "Toy Story," who was trained in hand-drawn animation and worked at Disney before joining Pixar. Now Doctor "draws" on the computer.

Analyst Keith Benjamin of Robertson, Stephens & Co, applauds Pixar's "key technology patents," but adds, "Its creative talent is its most important asset. The technology is second, and the distribution agreement with Disney is third." Sum it up and Benjamin rates Pixar stock a "buy."

In the deal Disney and Pixar reached in March, the two will jointly finance production of five more animated feature films which Pixar will produce and Disney market and distribute. But unlike with "Toy Story," the two will equally split profits from the movies and related merchandise, after Disney recoups its distribution costs. Disney also will invest more than $15 million in Pixar stock.
Pixar is working on a feature film, "A Bug's Life," for release in the fall of 1998, a video sequel to "Toy Story" also for 1998, and a third feature-length film it hopes to release in 2000.
